instructions: This repository is Oxidus, a MUD library written in LPC (Lars Pensjo C) targeting the FluffOS 2019+ driver. It is not C, C++, TypeScript, or any general-purpose language, and it is not an enterprise codebase — review it as a living, iteratively-developed, single-author game library. Read .claude/skills/lpc-review/SKILL.md in full before reviewing. It is the review standard for this repository and it governs: what qualifies as a finding, how scope is bounded to the change, how many findings to report, the evidence required before asserting a driver failure mode, and the LPC/FluffOS semantics most often mistaken for defects. Follow it as written. Two points from it carry the most weight here. First, scope: report a condition only if the change created it. A consumer that worked before the change and breaks after it is in scope wherever it lives, but pre-existing conditions, partial migrations, and code that does not yet match its eventual shape are states, not defects — every finding must state what the change did to cause the condition, and if that cannot be stated as a fact about the diff, the finding does not exist. Second, volume: report every qualifying finding in one pass, ordered strongest first, with no cap — withholding real defects to keep the list short turns one round of fixes into several. Volume is a consequence of the bar, never a target: no findings at all is the correct and expected outcome for most changes and is a complete review, not a failed one, so never reach for something to say. The context repo fluffos/fluffos is the C++ source of the driver this lib runs on. Use it as the authoritative reference for efun semantics and ground every driver-behaviour claim in that source rather than in C-language defaults, and never review it. There is no pinned driver version — the image is built from whatever upstream FluffOS was at build time — so the driver in front of you is authoritative: recent efuns, recent semantics, and language extensions added since the 2019 line are all fair to rely on, and code using them is not suspect for being recent.

rules.rule: New LPC source files must use the .lpc extension, not .c. The .c extension is legacy; the lib has fully migrated. Header files remain .h.

When guarding invocation of a closure/function pointer, prefer valid_function(f) over a bare functionp(f). functionp() alone is truthy even for closures whose owner has been destructed, which can crash at call time.
